finding.claim: deleteAccount discards the result of canDelete, so any authenticated non-admin user can delete another user's account by id.
finding.source: Path parameter id and the authenticated User u passed to deleteAccount (route DELETE /accounts/{id} per the comment on line 19; route wiring is not in the repo).
finding.sink: accounts.remove(id) at src/AccountService.java:23 (destructive deletion of another user's account).

trace.note: deleteAccount(User u, long id) receives the caller and the target id.
canDelete(u, a) is called but its boolean result is ignored, so no authorization takes effect.
accounts.remove(id) runs unconditionally, deleting the account regardless of ownership.

finding.guards_checked: canDelete (src/AccountService.java:9-11) implements admin-or-owner correctly but its result is unused on line 22. assertCanDelete (lines 13-17), which throws on failure, is not called in deleteAccount. closeAccount (lines 27-31) does call assertCanDelete, so the omission is specific to deleteAccount. No other guard exists in the file. Route-level authentication and authorization are not in the repo and could not be verified.

verdict.guard_found: None effective in deleteAccount. canDelete (src/AccountService.java:9-11) is correct, but its boolean is discarded as a bare statement at line 22. assertCanDelete (lines 13-17) is never called on the delete path; it is only called in closeAccount at line 29. Route-level auth for DELETE /accounts/{id} is not in the repo.
verdict.reason: At src/AccountService.java:22 the result of canDelete(u, a) is discarded, so line 23 (accounts.remove(id)) runs for any caller, while the correct check exists only in assertCanDelete (lines 13-17), which deleteAccount never calls; the attacker only needs to be a caller who passes a User object, and route-level access control, which is outside the repo, is the one thing that could still block this.

finding.claim: Distinguishable error responses reveal whether an account id exists: an unknown id triggers an NPE (500) for non-admin callers, while an existing account owned by someone else returns a SecurityException (403). Also deleteAccount NPEs on unknown ids.
finding.source: Path parameter id supplied by an authenticated non-admin caller.
finding.sink: Error response differences from accounts.get(id) returning null and the dereference a.ownerId() in canDelete (src/AccountService.java:10).

trace.note: accounts.get(id) returns null for a nonexistent id.
For a non-admin caller, a.ownerId() dereferences null and throws NullPointerException.
For an existing account owned by someone else, canDelete returns false and assertCanDelete throws SecurityException (403 in a typical mapping).

finding.guards_checked: No null check on the result of accounts.get in deleteAccount (line 21) or closeAccount (line 28). The admin short-circuit on line 10 avoids the NPE only for admins. Triage Check 8 (information-disclosure actionability) applies: the existence oracle is non-actionable on its own, so this is downgraded to LOW.

verdict.guard_found: The only guard on the deletion path is canDelete (src/AccountService.java:9-11), and deleteAccount discards its result at line 22, so it enforces nothing. closeAccount uses assertCanDelete (lines 13-17, 29), which does throw, so that path is guarded. No null check exists on accounts.get at lines 21 or 28.
verdict.reason: The trace misdescribes deleteAccount: at src/AccountService.java:22 the canDelete result is discarded, so it never throws SecurityException and any authenticated user can delete any existing account (ownership check bypassed, a more serious issue than the oracle claimed). The oracle claim is accurate only for closeAccount (lines 28-29), where an unknown id NPEs at line 10 for non-admins and an account owned by someone else throws SecurityException at line 15. Because the finding's trace and sink are wrong for the endpoint it names, it should be rejected as written and re-filed as a broken-authorization finding on deleteAccount:22.
